\\(\\delta\\).description: A small change or variation in a physical quantity.

temporal-invariance-law-16c94ce1.interpretation:
In this formula, 
\( \mathcal{L}(t) \n\)
 represents the Lagrangian of a physical system at a specific time 
\( t \n\)
. The term 
\( \mathcal{L}(t + \delta t) \n\)
 represents the Lagrangian of the same system at a later time 
\( t + \delta t \n\)
, where 
\( \delta t \n\)
 is an infinitesimally small interval of time. The equation 
\( \mathcal{L}(t) = \mathcal{L}(t + \delta t) \n\)
 asserts that the Lagrangian is the same at both times. This implies that the physical laws described by the Lagrangian, such as Newton's second law derived from the Euler-Lagrange equations, are independent of the absolute time.  If the Lagrangian depends explicitly on time, this temporal invariance is broken, and the system's dynamics would inherently depend on the specific time.
temporal-invariance-law-16c94ce1.limits_and_boundary:
This equation is an identity that holds for all valid times 
\( t \n\)
 and infinitesimal time differences 
\( \delta t \n\)
 for systems exhibiting temporal invariance. As 
\( \delta t \n\)
 approaches zero, the equation trivially becomes 
\( \mathcal{L}(t) = \mathcal{L}(t) \n\)
, which is always true. The significance lies in the requirement that the Lagrangian must not have an explicit dependence on 
\( t \n\)
 for this identity to hold for all 
\( t \n\)
 and 
\( \delta t \n\)
. If 
\( \mathcal{L} \n\)
 depends explicitly on 
\( t \n\)
, this temporal invariance is broken.
temporal-invariance-law-16c94ce1.conceptual_definition:
The Temporal Invariance Law, mathematically expressed as 
\( 
\mathcal{L}(t) = \mathcal{L}(t + \delta t) \n\)

states that the Lagrangian, denoted by 
\( 
\mathcal{L} \n\)

of a physical system remains unchanged regardless of when it is evaluated in time. This means that the physical laws governing the system's dynamics do not depend on the absolute time, but rather on the time intervals and the relative evolution of the system's configuration. The Lagrangian is typically defined as the difference between the kinetic energy (
\( T \n\)
) and the potential energy (
\( V \n\)
) of the system, so 
\( 
\mathcal{L} = T - V \n\)
. If 
\( \mathcal{L} \n\)
 is invariant under a time translation by an arbitrary infinitesimal amount 
\( \delta t \n\)
, it implies that the system's dynamics are independent of the specific moment in time at which the observation is made.
temporal-invariance-law-16c94ce1.intuitive_summary: The system behaves identically at any point in time, meaning its fundamental equations of motion do not change with the passage of absolute time.

projection-law-e10e1572.title: Projection Law

|\u03c8'}.name: Projected and Normalized Quantum State
|\u03c8'}.description: The resulting quantum state after projecting the initial state |ψ} onto a specific subspace or eigenstate, and then normalizing it to be a valid quantum state (i.e., with unit norm).

\u0089_n.name: Projection Operator
\u0089_n.description: An operator that projects a quantum state vector onto a specific subspace or eigenstate. If |φ_n} is a normalized eigenstate, the projection operator is often written as _n = |φ_n}<φ_n|.

|\u03c8}.name: Initial Quantum State
|\u03c8}.description: The arbitrary quantum state of the system before the projection operation is applied. It is a vector in the Hilbert space of the system.

P_n.name: Probability (or related scalar)
P_n.description: The eigenvalue associated with the projection operator _n. In many contexts, especially when _n is a projection onto a single eigenstate |φ_n}, this eigenvalue corresponds to the probability of finding the system in the state |φ_n} if the initial state was |ψ}. Specifically, if _n = |φ_n}<φ_n|, then the eigenvalue is <ψ|_n|ψ} = |<φ_n|ψ}|², which is the probability.

\\(\\psi\\).name: Quantum Wavefunction
\\(\\psi\\).description: A complex wavefunction describing the probability amplitude of a quantum state.

\\(x\\).name: Position / Displacement
\\(x\\).description: A coordinate representing the location of a particle along a specific axis, or the displacement from an equilibrium position.

\\(P\\).name: Pressure
\\(P\\).description: The perpendicular force exerted per unit area on the boundary of a system.

\\(n\\).name: Refractive Index / Particle Density
\\(n\\).description: The ratio of speed of light in vacuum to that in a medium, or particles per unit volume.

projection-law-e10e1572.interpretation: In this formula, |ψ} represents an arbitrary initial quantum state of a system. The term _n is a projection operator. If |φ_n} is an eigenstate of some observable, then _n|ψ} effectively isolates the component of |ψ} that lies in the direction of |φ_n} (or the subspace spanned by it). The value _n is the eigenvalue corresponding to the projection operator, which is related to the probability of the state |ψ} being found in the projected state. The square root of _n in the denominator is a normalization factor. When _n is a projection operator onto a single state |φ_n}, the projection operator is _n = |φ_n}}<φ_n|. In this case, _n|ψ} = |φ_n}<φ_n|ψ}. The quantity <φ_n|ψ} is the amplitude for the state |ψ} to be found in the state |φ_n}. The probability of this occurrence is |<φ_n|ψ}|². The formula as written seems to imply _n is the eigenvalue related to probability, and the projection operator is implicitly assumed to be normalized in a way that the eigenvalue is the probability itself or a related scalar factor. If _n is interpreted as the probability, then |ψ'} represents the new, normalized quantum state after the projection, effectively capturing the state conditioned on the outcome associated with the projection.
projection-law-e10e1572.symmetry_origin: This law arises from the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics, particularly the Born rule for probability interpretation and the postulate of state evolution or measurement. In the context of measurement, when an observable is measured, the quantum state collapses onto one of its eigenstates. The projection operator formalism precisely describes this process, projecting the initial state onto the subspace corresponding to the measured eigenvalue. It's a consequence of the Hilbert space structure and the linear nature of quantum operators.
projection-law-e10e1572.limits_and_boundary: If the projection operator _n represents the projection onto a state |φ_n} that is orthogonal to the initial state |ψ} (i.e., <φ_n|ψ} = 0), then the projection _n|ψ} = 0. In this case, the resulting state |ψ'} would be a null vector, indicating zero probability of finding the system in that state. If the initial state |ψ} is already an eigenstate of the observable corresponding to _n, then _n|ψ} = _n|ψ}, where _n is the eigenvalue. If this eigenvalue is 1 (for a normalized projection onto itself), the resulting state |ψ'} would be equal to |ψ} itself, up to normalization.
projection-law-e10e1572.conceptual_definition: The Projection Law in quantum mechanics describes how a quantum state, represented by a ket vector |ψ}, is transformed when one considers the probability of finding it in a specific subspace or associated with a particular observable outcome. Specifically, if |ψ} is a general quantum state and |φ_n} is an eigenstate of some observable , then the projection of |ψ} onto |φ_n}, normalized to yield a state, is given by the formula. The operator _n represents the projection operator onto the subspace spanned by the eigenstate |φ_n}, and _n is the corresponding eigenvalue representing the probability (or related quantity) of finding the system in that state.
projection-law-e10e1572.intuitive_summary: This law states that the new state after projection is the original state's component along a specific direction, normalized to represent a valid quantum state.

four-velocity-acceleration-orthogonality.title: Velocity-Acceleration Orthogonality
four-velocity-acceleration-orthogonality.interpretation:
In this equation, $U^\mu$ represents the four-velocity of an object, which is a four-vector combining the object's three-dimensional velocity and its time rate of change. The components of the four-velocity are typically given by $U^\mu = \gamma(c, v_x, v_y, v_z)$, where $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$ is the Lorentz factor, $v$ is the magnitude of the three-velocity, and $c$ is the speed of light. The symbol $a_\mu$ represents the covariant four-acceleration, which is the four-vector describing the rate of change of the four-velocity with respect to proper time. In a flat spacetime (Minkowski spacetime), the components of the four-acceleration are related to the ordinary acceleration and velocity. The equation $U^\mu a_\mu = 0$ is an expression for the inner product of these two four-vectors using the Minkowski metric. The inner product is defined as $U^\mu a_\mu = \eta_{\mu
u} U^\mu a^
u$, where $\eta_{\mu
u}$ is the Minkowski metric tensor. The result being zero signifies that the four-velocity and four-acceleration are orthogonal in Minkowski spacetime. This orthogonality is a direct consequence of the constancy of the magnitude of the four-velocity for massive particles, which is always $U^\mu U_\mu = c^2$ (or $c$ in units where $c=1$). Differentiating this constancy with respect to proper time yields $U^\mu a_\mu = 0$.
four-velocity-acceleration-orthogonality.conceptual_definition: The equation $U^\mu a_\mu = 0$ expresses a fundamental relationship in relativistic physics, specifically within the framework of four-vectors. It states that the inner product of an object's four-velocity and its four-acceleration is zero. This orthogonality implies that changes in an object's velocity (acceleration) are always perpendicular to its velocity itself in spacetime. This concept is crucial for understanding how objects move under the influence of forces in a way that is consistent with the principles of special relativity.
four-velocity-acceleration-orthogonality.intuitive_summary: In spacetime, an object's acceleration is always perpendicular to its velocity.
four-velocity-acceleration-orthogonality.symmetry_origin: This relationship arises from the kinematic constraint that a massive particle must always travel at a speed less than the speed of light, implying that the magnitude of its four-velocity in spacetime is constant ($U^\mu U_\mu = c^2$). Differentiating this invariant with respect to proper time, and using the definition of four-acceleration ($a_\mu = dU_\mu/d\tau$), directly leads to the orthogonality condition $U^\mu a_\mu = 0$. This is a consequence of the Lorentz symmetry of spacetime, as it holds regardless of the observer's inertial frame of reference.
four-velocity-acceleration-orthogonality.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit, where the velocity $v \to 0$, the Lorentz factor $\gamma \to 1$. The four-velocity approaches $(c, 0, 0, 0)$ and the four-acceleration's time component approaches 0 (since it's related to the time derivative of $\gamma$, which is proportional to $v^2$ for small $v$), while its spatial components are the ordinary three-acceleration. The orthogonality condition still holds, but its interpretation simplifies to the fact that the time component of acceleration is negligible compared to its spatial components in this limit, and the time component of velocity is dominant.

U^\\mu.name: Four-velocity
U^\\mu.description: The relativistic velocity four-vector of an object, which combines its three-dimensional velocity with a time component related to the speed of light. Its magnitude squared is a spacetime invariant, equal to $c^2$ for massive particles.

a_\\mu.name: Four-acceleration
a_\\mu.description: The relativistic acceleration four-vector, representing the rate of change of the four-velocity with respect to proper time. Its components are related to the ordinary three-acceleration and the rate of change of the Lorentz factor.

\\mu.name: Spacetime Index
\\mu.description: An index that runs over the dimensions of spacetime. In special relativity, \mu ranges from 0 to 3, where 0 typically represents the time dimension and 1, 2, 3 represent the spatial dimensions.

c.name: Speed of Light
c.description: The universal constant representing the speed of light in a vacuum, approximately $299,792,458$ m/s.

\\(U\\).name: Potential Energy
\\(U\\).description: Position-dependent stored energy of a system.

\\(a\\).name: Acceleration Magnitude
\\(a\\).description: The rate of change of speed or velocity magnitude with respect to time.

ontology-identity-1-8fc2010b.title: CHSH Bell Inequality
ontology-identity-1-8fc2010b.interpretation: The CHSH Bell Inequality is expressed as \(|E(a,b) - E(a,b') + E(a',b) + E(a',b')| \leq 2\). Here, \(a\) and \(a'\) represent two different measurement settings for observer A, and \(b\) and \(b'\) represent two different measurement settings for observer B. The term \(E(a,b)\) denotes the expectation value (average correlation) of the measurement outcomes when observer A chooses setting \(a\) and observer B chooses setting \(b\). These expectation values are typically calculated based on the joint probability distributions of the measurement outcomes. For instance, if the measurements are spin projections along certain axes, \(E(a,b)\) would be the average product of the spin projections measured by A and B. The inequality is a crucial test for quantum mechanics, as quantum mechanics predicts violations of this inequality in certain scenarios involving entangled particles, indicating that local realism is not a complete description of reality at the quantum level.
ontology-identity-1-8fc2010b.symmetry_origin: The CHSH Bell Inequality is derived from the principle of local realism. Local realism is a philosophical and physical assumption stating that: 1) Locality: Physical influences cannot propagate faster than the speed of light. 2) Realism: Physical systems possess definite properties that exist independently of whether they are measured. The derivation involves considering all possible joint probability distributions consistent with local realism for the outcomes of measurements made at spatially separated locations. The inequality emerges as a necessary condition for any such local realistic theory.
ontology-identity-1-8fc2010b.limits_and_boundary: The value of the expression \(|E(a,b) - E(a,b') + E(a',b) + E(a',b')|\) is bounded by 2 for any theory adhering to local realism. Quantum mechanics, however, can predict values up to \(2√{2}\) (approximately 2.828) for certain entangled states and measurement settings. Therefore, observing a value greater than 2 experimentally would indicate a violation of local realism, favoring quantum mechanics' non-local and non-realist description of nature. The boundary value of 2 represents the limit imposed by classical, local, and realist physical theories.

E(a,b).name: Expectation Value
E(a,b).description: The expectation value of the product of measurement outcomes when observer A chooses setting 'a' and observer B chooses setting 'b'. This represents the average correlation between their respective measurements.

a.name: Measurement Setting A1
a.description: The first choice of measurement setting for observer A. This could represent, for example, the angle of a polarizer or the direction of a spin measurement.

a'.name: Measurement Setting A2
a'.description: The second choice of measurement setting for observer A, distinct from setting 'a'.

b.name: Measurement Setting B1
b.description: The first choice of measurement setting for observer B. This could represent, for example, the angle of a polarizer or the direction of a spin measurement.

b'.name: Measurement Setting B2
b'.description: The second choice of measurement setting for observer B, distinct from setting 'b'.

\\(E\\).name: Electric Field Strength
\\(E\\).description: The magnitude of the electric field vector, representing the force per unit charge at a point in space.

\\(x\\).name: Position / Displacement
\\(x\\).description: A coordinate representing the location of a particle along a specific axis, or the displacement from an equilibrium position.

ontology-identity-1-8fc2010b.conceptual_definition: The CHSH Bell Inequality is a mathematical statement that sets an upper bound on the correlations between measurement outcomes of two spatially separated observers, assuming that these outcomes are determined by local hidden variables. It is derived from the assumption of local realism, which posits that physical properties exist independently of measurement and that influences cannot travel faster than the speed of light.  The inequality states that if local realism holds true, a specific combination of correlations between different measurement settings must be less than or equal to 2.
ontology-identity-1-8fc2010b.intuitive_summary: If the universe is local and real, the correlations between measurements on entangled particles at different angles must satisfy a specific limit.

perturbative-metric-tensor.title: Perturbative Metric Tensor
perturbative-metric-tensor.conceptual_definition: The formula represents the metric tensor in a spacetime that is close to flat, typically used in the weak field limit of General Relativity. It decomposes the full metric tensor, which describes the geometry of spacetime, into a background flat spacetime metric and a small perturbation term.
perturbative-metric-tensor.intuitive_summary: This equation states that a slightly curved spacetime can be understood by starting with a flat spacetime and adding a small correction.
perturbative-metric-tensor.interpretation:
In this equation, the term \( g_{\mu
u} \) is the metric tensor, a fundamental object in differential geometry and physics that defines distances and time intervals in a spacetime manifold. It is a symmetric (0,2)-tensor. The term \( \eta_{\mu
u} \) represents the Minkowski metric tensor, which is the metric of flat, featureless spacetime in special relativity. In Cartesian coordinates, it is a diagonal matrix with entries (+1, -1, -1, -1) or (-1, +1, +1, +1) depending on convention. The term \( h_{\mu
u} \) is the perturbation term, which is assumed to be small and represents the deviation of the actual spacetime geometry from flatness. This deviation is what accounts for the presence of mass and energy, and thus gravity, in General Relativity. The equation fundamentally expresses the idea that in regions of weak gravitational fields, the geometry of spacetime is only slightly different from that of flat spacetime.
perturbative-metric-tensor.symmetry_origin: This formulation arises directly from the principles of General Relativity, specifically in the weak-field approximation. When gravitational fields are weak (i.e., when the spacetime is nearly flat), Einstein's field equations can be linearized. This linearization process leads to describing the gravitational field in terms of small perturbations \( h_{\mu\nu} \) on top of the flat Minkowski background \( \eta_{\mu\nu} \). This approach is crucial for understanding phenomena like gravitational waves and the behavior of objects in the Solar System (excluding extreme cases).
perturbative-metric-tensor.limits_and_boundary:
As the gravitational field becomes weaker, the perturbation \( h_{\mu
u} \) approaches the zero tensor. In this limit, \( g_{\mu
u} 	o \eta_{\mu
u} \), meaning the spacetime becomes exactly flat, corresponding to Special Relativity. Conversely, as the gravitational field becomes stronger, \( h_{\mu
u} \) becomes larger, and the linear approximation breaks down, requiring the full non-linear Einstein field equations to describe the spacetime geometry.

g_{\\mu\\nu}.name: Metric Tensor
g_{\\mu\\nu}.description: The metric tensor of the spacetime, which defines the interval ds^2 = g_{\mu\nu} dx^{\mu} dx^{\nu} and thus the geometry of spacetime. It is a symmetric tensor of rank 2.

\\eta_{\\mu\\nu}.name: Minkowski Metric Tensor
\\eta_{\\mu\\nu}.description: The metric tensor of flat spacetime in special relativity. In standard Cartesian coordinates, it is diag(+1, -1, -1, -1) or diag(-1, +1, +1, +1).

h_{\\mu\\nu}.name: Metric Perturbation
h_{\\mu\\nu}.description: The small perturbation to the Minkowski metric, representing the deviation from flatness due to the presence of mass-energy and hence gravity. It is a symmetric tensor of rank 2.

phase-velocity.title: Phase velocity
phase-velocity.conceptual_definition:
The phase velocity, denoted by 
(v_p)
, is the velocity at which a specific phase of a wave propagates in space. For example, it is the speed at which the crest of a sinusoidal wave travels. This is distinct from the group velocity, which describes the speed at which the overall envelope of the wave's amplitude, or energy, propagates.
phase-velocity.intuitive_summary: The phase velocity is the ratio of a wave's angular frequency to its wave number, indicating how fast a point of constant phase moves.
phase-velocity.interpretation:
The formula 
(v_p = \omega/k)
 defines the phase velocity 
(v_p)
 as the quotient of the angular frequency 
(\omega)
 and the wave number 
(k)
. The angular frequency 
(\omega)
 represents the rate of oscillation of the wave in time, measured in radians per second (rad/s). The wave number 
(k)
, on the other hand, quantifies the spatial periodicity of the wave, representing the number of radians per unit length, typically measured in inverse meters (m⁻¹).  The ratio of these two quantities directly yields the speed at which a point of constant phase (like a crest or trough) traverses space. A higher angular frequency for a given wave number implies a faster phase velocity, and a smaller wave number for a given angular frequency also implies a faster phase velocity.
phase-velocity.symmetry_origin:
This formula arises from the fundamental description of monochromatic waves using Fourier analysis, where waves are represented by sinusoidal functions of space and time, such as 
(A \cos(kx - \omega t))
. A point of constant phase satisfies 
(kx - \omega t = \text{constant})
. Differentiating with respect to time 
(t)
, we get 
(k \frac{dx}{dt} - \omega = 0)
, which rearranges to 
(\frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{\omega}{k})
. Thus, the velocity of this constant phase point, the phase velocity, is 
(v_p = \omega/k)
. It is fundamentally tied to the translational symmetry in space and time that characterizes wave propagation.
phase-velocity.limits_and_boundary:
As the wave number 
(k)
 approaches zero (long wavelength limit), the phase velocity tends to infinity, assuming a finite angular frequency 
(\omega)
. This scenario corresponds to a wave that is almost uniform in space. Conversely, as the angular frequency 
(\omega)
 approaches zero (static limit, although technically not a propagating wave), the phase velocity approaches zero, assuming a finite wave number 
(k)
. If both 
(\omega)
 and 
(k)
 approach zero simultaneously, the limit depends on the specific relationship between them, which defines the dispersion relation of the wave medium.

v_p.name: Phase Velocity
v_p.description: The speed at which a particular phase of a wave travels through space.

\\omega.name: Angular Frequency
\\omega.description: The rate of change of the phase of a wave in time, measured in radians per second.

k.name: Wave Number
k.description: The spatial frequency of the wave, representing the number of radians per unit length.

parallel-magnetic-field-continuity.title: Parallel magnetic field continuity
parallel-magnetic-field-continuity.conceptual_definition: This formula, known as the magnetic boundary condition for the tangential component of the magnetic field, states that the component of the magnetic field vector tangent to an interface between two different magnetic media remains continuous across that interface. This continuity arises from a fundamental property of magnetic fields related to the absence of magnetic monopoles and the structure of Ampere's law in integral form.
parallel-magnetic-field-continuity.intuitive_summary: The magnetic field's tendency to 'flow' parallel to a boundary means its tangential component doesn't abruptly change when crossing from one material to another.
parallel-magnetic-field-continuity.interpretation: The equation $H_{1	op} = H_{2	op}$ describes the behavior of the magnetic field intensity vector, often denoted as $\vec{H}$, at the interface between two distinct magnetic materials, labeled region 1 and region 2. The subscript $\top$ indicates the component of the magnetic field intensity that is tangential (parallel) to the boundary surface.  Therefore, $H_{1	op}$ represents the tangential component of $\vec{H}$ in medium 1, and $H_{2	op}$ represents the tangential component of $\vec{H}$ in medium 2, immediately adjacent to the interface. The equality signifies that this tangential component does not change abruptly as one moves across the boundary. This condition is derived from considering a small rectangular Amperian loop that straddles the boundary, with two sides parallel to the boundary and two sides perpendicular to it.  In the limit as the perpendicular sides shrink to zero length, the integral of $\vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l}$ around this loop reduces to the difference in tangential components across the boundary, which must be zero in the absence of surface currents.
parallel-magnetic-field-continuity.symmetry_origin: This condition is a direct consequence of Ampere's Law in its integral form, $\oint \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l} = I_{enc}$. When applied to a path enclosing an interface between two media that does not have free surface current densities ($\vec{K}$), the enclosed current $I_{enc}$ is zero. For a path that is infinitesimally thin in the direction perpendicular to the interface, the integral simplifies to the difference between the tangential components of $\vec{H}$ on either side of the interface. Since this difference must be zero, the tangential components are continuous.
parallel-magnetic-field-continuity.limits_and_boundary: In the absence of free surface current densities ($\vec{K}$) at the interface, the tangential component of $\vec{H}$ is continuous, meaning $H_{1	op} = H_{2	op}$ irrespective of the properties of the two magnetic materials (e.g., permeability). If there were a surface current density $K$ flowing along the boundary, the condition would be modified to $H_{2	op} - H_{1	op} = \vec{K} \times \hat{n}$, where $\hat{n}$ is a unit vector normal to the surface pointing from medium 1 to medium 2. In the limit of infinite permeability for both materials (which is a hypothetical scenario as permeabilities are finite), this condition would still hold if there are no surface currents.

H_{1\\parallel}.name: Tangential Component of Magnetic Field Intensity in Medium 1
H_{1\\parallel}.description: The component of the magnetic field intensity vector \(\vec{H}\) that is parallel (tangent) to the interface separating two magnetic media, as measured in medium 1.

H_{2\\parallel}.name: Tangential Component of Magnetic Field Intensity in Medium 2
H_{2\\parallel}.description: The component of the magnetic field intensity vector \(\vec{H}\) that is parallel (tangent) to the interface separating two magnetic media, as measured in medium 2.

time-evolution-hamiltonian-poisson-brack.title: Time Evolution in Hamiltonian Mechanics (Poisson Bracket)
time-evolution-hamiltonian-poisson-brack.conceptual_definition: The equation describes the time evolution of any physical observable, represented by the quantity $A$, within the framework of Hamiltonian mechanics. It states that the total rate of change of $A$ with respect to time is the sum of its explicit time dependence and its dependence on the Hamiltonian $H$, mediated by the Poisson bracket operation.
time-evolution-hamiltonian-poisson-brack.intuitive_summary: The rate of change of any physical quantity over time is determined by how it explicitly depends on time plus how it interacts with the system's total energy (Hamiltonian) through a structure called the Poisson bracket.
time-evolution-hamiltonian-poisson-brack.interpretation: The equation $\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{\partial A}{\partial t} + \{A, H\}$ governs the time evolution of an observable $A$ in Hamiltonian mechanics. The term $\frac{dA}{dt}$ represents the total rate of change of $A$ as observed over time. The term $\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}$ accounts for any explicit dependence of the observable $A$ on time itself, independent of the system's dynamics. For instance, if $A$ were a time-dependent measuring device's reading, this term would capture that. The term $\{A, H\}$ is the Poisson bracket of $A$ with the Hamiltonian $H$. The Poisson bracket is a fundamental operation in classical mechanics that measures how $A$ changes as the system evolves according to the Hamiltonian. Specifically, for generalized coordinates $q_i$ and conjugate momenta $p_i$, the Poisson bracket is defined as $\{A, H\} = \sum_i \left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} - \frac{\partial A}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i}\right)$. This term encapsulates the implicit time evolution of $A$ due to the system's dynamics governed by $H$. If $A$ is a conserved quantity, its time derivative $\frac{dA}{dt}$ is zero, and if it has no explicit time dependence ($\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = 0$), then $\{A, H\} = 0$, meaning $A$ commutes with the Hamiltonian.
time-evolution-hamiltonian-poisson-brack.symmetry_origin: This equation is a direct consequence of Hamilton's equations of motion, which are derived from the principle of least action and are invariant under canonical transformations. The Poisson bracket formalism provides a powerful way to express these dynamics, highlighting the structure of phase space and its symmetries. The conservation of energy, for example, arises when the Hamiltonian $H$ is time-independent, leading to $\frac{dH}{dt} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + \{H, H\} = 0 + 0 = 0$.
time-evolution-hamiltonian-poisson-brack.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the Hamiltonian $H$ is zero (no energy or interactions), the time evolution of $A$ is solely determined by its explicit time dependence: $\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{\partial A}{\partial t}$. If an observable $A$ has no explicit time dependence ($\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = 0$) and commutes with the Hamiltonian (i.e., $\{A, H\} = 0$, meaning $A$ is a conserved quantity), then its time derivative is zero: $\frac{dA}{dt} = 0$, indicating that $A$ remains constant throughout the evolution of the system.

A.name: Observable
A.description: A physical observable quantity (e.g., position, momentum, energy, angular momentum) whose time evolution is being studied. It is generally a function of the generalized coordinates, generalized momenta, and possibly time.

dA/dt.name: Total Time Derivative of Observable
dA/dt.description: The total rate of change of the observable A with respect to time, considering both its explicit time dependence and its dependence on the evolving system variables.

\\partial A / \\partial t.name: Partial Time Derivative of Observable
\\partial A / \\partial t.description: The explicit rate of change of the observable A with respect to time, assuming the system's generalized coordinates and momenta are held constant. This represents how A changes intrinsically with time, independent of the system's dynamics.

\\{A, H\\}.name: Poisson Bracket of A and H
\\{A, H\\}.description: The Poisson bracket between the observable A and the Hamiltonian H. It quantifies how A changes as a function of the system's generalized coordinates and momenta, which are governed by H. Mathematically, for generalized coordinates $q_i$ and momenta $p_i$, it is defined as $\sum_i \left(\frac{\partial A}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} - \frac{\partial A}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i}\right)$.

H.name: Hamiltonian
H.description: The Hamiltonian of the system, which typically represents the total energy of the system as a function of generalized coordinates, generalized momenta, and possibly time. It governs the system's dynamics via Hamilton's equations.

cosine-taylor-expansion.title: Taylor expansion of cosine
cosine-taylor-expansion.conceptual_definition:
The Taylor expansion of cosine provides a polynomial approximation for the cosine function, particularly useful for small angular values. Specifically, the formula 
$$ \cos \theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} $$
 represents the first two non-zero terms of the Maclaurin series expansion of \( \cos \theta \). This approximation is highly accurate when the angle \( \theta \) is close to zero radians.
cosine-taylor-expansion.intuitive_summary: For very small angles, the cosine function behaves almost like a simple quadratic curve, starting at 1 and decreasing symmetrically.
cosine-taylor-expansion.interpretation: In this approximation, \( \cos \theta \) is represented by a polynomial in terms of the angle \( \theta \). The term '1' represents the value of \( \cos \theta \) at \( \theta = 0 \). The term \( -\frac{\theta^2}{2} \) accounts for the initial curvature of the cosine function as the angle deviates from zero. As \( \theta \) increases, higher-order terms from the full Taylor series (\( \frac{\theta^4}{4!} \), \( -\frac{\theta^6}{6!} \), etc.) become necessary for a more accurate representation. This approximation is particularly powerful in physics when dealing with small oscillations, wave phenomena, or small perturbations where trigonometric functions can be simplified to algebraic expressions, leading to simpler differential equations and analytical solutions.
cosine-taylor-expansion.symmetry_origin: The Taylor expansion of \( \cos \theta \) originates from the fundamental properties of the cosine function, which is an even function, meaning \( \cos(-\theta) = \cos(\theta) \). This symmetry is reflected in its Maclaurin series, which only contains even powers of \( \theta \) (\( \theta^0, \theta^2, \theta^4, \dots \)). The coefficients of the series are derived from the derivatives of \( \cos \theta \) evaluated at \( \theta = 0 \): \( \cos(0)=1 \), \( \frac{d}{d\theta}(\cos \theta)|_{\theta=0} = 0 \), \( \frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}(\cos \theta)|_{\theta=0} = -1 \), and so on. The approximation \( \cos \theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} \) utilizes the first two non-zero terms of this series.
cosine-taylor-expansion.limits_and_boundary: As \( \theta \to 0 \) (approaches zero), the term \( \frac{\theta^2}{2} \) also approaches zero, so \( \cos \theta \to 1 \), which is the exact value of \( \cos(0) \). The approximation becomes increasingly accurate as \( \theta \) gets closer to zero. For large values of \( \theta \), this approximation rapidly loses accuracy, and higher-order terms of the Taylor series are required for a meaningful representation. The cosine function itself oscillates between -1 and 1, a behavior not captured by this truncated series for large \( \theta \).

\\cos \\theta.name: Cosine of the angle
\\cos \\theta.description: The value of the cosine function for a given angle \( \theta \). In the context of the Taylor expansion, this represents the function being approximated.

\\theta.name: Angle
\\theta.description: The angle in radians. This is the independent variable in the Taylor expansion. The approximation is most accurate for small values of \( \theta \).

equation-of-state-limit.title: Equation of state parameter limit
equation-of-state-limit.conceptual_definition: The expression \( w \to -1 \) signifies a limit in cosmology, specifically describing the equation of state parameter of a substance or field. The parameter \( w \) is the ratio of its pressure \( p \) to its energy density \( \rho \), i.e., \( w = p/\rho \). The limit \( w \to -1 \) is of profound importance as it corresponds to a substance that drives the accelerated expansion of the universe, such as a cosmological constant or dark energy.
equation-of-state-limit.intuitive_summary: This limit indicates a substance with negative pressure that causes the universe to expand at an ever-increasing rate.
equation-of-state-limit.interpretation: In this context, \( w \) is the equation of state parameter, a dimensionless quantity defined as the ratio of pressure \( p \) to energy density \( \rho \) for a homogeneous and isotropic fluid or field. The relationship \( w = p/\rho \) dictates how the energy density of this component evolves as the universe expands. The limit \( w \to -1 \) is particularly significant because it describes a 'cosmological constant'-like behavior. For such a component, the pressure is negative and equal in magnitude to its energy density, \( p = -\rho \). This negative pressure leads to a repulsive gravitational effect, causing the expansion of the universe to accelerate, as described by the Friedmann equations in the context of general relativity.
equation-of-state-limit.symmetry_origin: The equation of state parameter \( w \) arises from the stress-energy tensor of a perfect fluid in general relativity. The specific limit \( w \to -1 \) is not derived from a symmetry but rather from the observed accelerated expansion of the universe, which is best explained by a component with this equation of state. This behavior is consistent with a cosmological constant, which is invariant under spacetime translations and rotations, reflecting a fundamental property of spacetime itself rather than a dynamic field.
equation-of-state-limit.limits_and_boundary: When \( w \to -1 \), the component behaves like a cosmological constant. Its energy density \( \rho \) remains constant as the universe expands, unlike matter (where \( w=0 \)) or radiation (where \( w=1/3 \)). This constant energy density drives accelerated expansion. If \( w \to 0 \), the component behaves like non-relativistic matter, and its energy density dilutes as \( a^{-3} \) where \( a \) is the scale factor. If \( w \to 1/3 \), it behaves like relativistic matter (radiation), and its energy density dilutes as \( a^{-4} \).

w.name: Equation of State Parameter
w.description: A dimensionless parameter representing the ratio of pressure \( p \) to energy density \( \rho \) for a component in the universe. The limit \( w \to -1 \) implies a constant energy density and accelerated expansion.

p.name: Pressure
p.description: The thermodynamic pressure exerted by the component. In the limit \( w \to -1 \), the pressure is negative and equal in magnitude to the energy density.

\\rho.name: Energy Density
\\rho.description: The amount of energy per unit volume of the component. For \( w \to -1 \), \( \rho \) remains constant over time, a characteristic of dark energy or a cosmological constant.

zero-total-momentum-cm.title: Zero total momentum in CM frame
zero-total-momentum-cm.conceptual_definition: The equation ∑ m_i \mathbf{v}'_i = 0 states that the total momentum of a system of particles, when measured in its center-of-mass (CM) frame, is always zero. This means that the vector sum of the individual momenta of all particles in the system, weighted by their respective masses, cancels out in this specific reference frame.
zero-total-momentum-cm.intuitive_summary: In the center-of-mass frame, the total momentum of the system is always zero because the frame is defined by the system's overall motion, implying no net external momentum.
zero-total-momentum-cm.interpretation: The formula ∑ m_i \mathbf{v}'_i = 0 describes the total momentum of a system of particles within the center-of-mass (CM) frame. Here, \( m_i \) represents the mass of the \( i \)-th particle in the system, typically measured in kilograms (kg). The term \( \mathbf{v}'_i \) denotes the velocity of the \( i \)-th particle as observed from the CM frame, measured in meters per second (m/s). The prime (') indicates that the velocity is relative to the CM frame. The summation symbol \( \sum \) signifies that we sum the product of each particle's mass and its velocity in the CM frame over all particles \( i \) in the system. The equation asserts that this total vector sum of momenta is identically zero, \( = 0 \). This implies that for every particle moving with a certain momentum in the CM frame, there must be other particles or combinations of particles whose momenta exactly cancel it out, resulting in no net momentum for the entire system.
zero-total-momentum-cm.symmetry_origin: This equation originates from the definition of the center-of-mass frame itself. The center-of-mass frame is defined as the inertial reference frame in which the total linear momentum of the system is zero. Mathematically, if \( \mathbf{v}_{CM} \) is the velocity of the center of mass of the system, then the CM frame is the frame where \( \mathbf{v}_{CM} = \frac{\sum m_i \mathbf{v}_i}{\sum m_i} = 0 \), which directly implies \( \sum m_i \mathbf{v}_i = 0 \). In a more general setting, it arises from the conservation of linear momentum. If the system is isolated (no external forces), its total momentum is conserved. Choosing the CM frame as the reference frame simplifies analysis because the total momentum is constant and, by definition of the CM frame, that constant is zero.
zero-total-momentum-cm.limits_and_boundary: As the number of particles \( N \) approaches infinity, while maintaining a finite total mass and momentum, the individual velocities \( \mathbf{v}'_i \) in the CM frame would tend to become smaller, such that their weighted sum remains zero. If the system contains only a single particle \( (N=1) \), then \( m_1 \mathbf{v}'_1 = 0 \). Since \( m_1 \) is non-zero, this implies \( \mathbf{v}'_1 = 0 \). This means that if a system consists of only one particle, the CM frame is the rest frame of that particle. If all particles have zero velocity in the CM frame (i.e., \( \mathbf{v}'_i = 0 \) for all \( i \)), then the total momentum is trivially zero, indicating that the entire system is at rest in the CM frame.

\\( m_i \\).description: The mass of the i-th particle in the system. This is a scalar quantity representing the inertia of the particle.

\\( \\mathbf{v}'_i \\).name: Velocity of particle i in the CM frame
\\( \\mathbf{v}'_i \\).description: The velocity vector of the i-th particle as measured in the center-of-mass (CM) reference frame. The prime (') indicates that the velocity is relative to the CM frame.

\\( \\sum \\).name: Summation
\\( \\sum \\).description: The mathematical operator indicating the sum of the terms that follow for all particles in the system.

\\( 0 \\).name: Zero vector
\\( 0 \\).description: Represents the zero vector in three-dimensional space, indicating that the total momentum of the system in the center-of-mass frame has no magnitude and no direction.

proper-time-curved-spacetime.title: Proper time calculation in curved spacetime
proper-time-curved-spacetime.conceptual_definition: The formula calculates the proper time elapsed along a worldline in a curved spacetime. Proper time is the time measured by an observer moving along that worldline, experiencing the effects of gravity as curvature of spacetime. It is an invariant quantity, meaning it is independent of the coordinate system used to describe the spacetime.
proper-time-curved-spacetime.intuitive_summary: Proper time is the physically experienced duration along a path through spacetime, independent of external observers' measurements.
proper-time-curved-spacetime.interpretation: The formula for proper time 	au in curved spacetime is given by 	au = ∫_{λ1}^{λ2} √{-g_{μν} \frac{dx^μ}{dλ} \frac{dx^ν}{dλ}} dλ}. Here, λ is an arbitrary affine parameter along the worldline of an object. The term \frac{dx^μ}{dλ} represents the tangent vector to the worldline in spacetime, indicating the object's displacement in each coordinate direction per unit of the parameter λ. The metric tensor 2g_{μν}3 describes the geometry of spacetime, defining distances and time intervals. The product 2-g_{μν} \frac{dx^μ}{dλ} \frac{dx^ν}{dλ}3 is the square of the infinitesimal proper time element (ds^2) along the worldline, where the negative sign is conventionally used for timelike or null paths in relativistic physics (assuming a mostly plus signature convention for the metric). The integral sums up these infinitesimal proper time intervals along the path from the initial parameter value λ1 to the final parameter value λ2, yielding the total proper time experienced by the object.
proper-time-curved-spacetime.symmetry_origin: This formula is a direct consequence of the principles of general relativity, particularly the concept of spacetime as a pseudo-Riemannian manifold. The invariance of proper time under coordinate transformations (coordinate independence) is a fundamental tenet. It arises from the need for a physical quantity (time experienced by an observer) to be independent of the arbitrary labeling of spacetime events (coordinates). Mathematically, it is derived from the spacetime interval ds^2 = g_{μν} dx^μ dx^ν, where for timelike or null paths, ds^2 is related to the proper time by ds^2 = -c^2 d	au^2 (with c=1 in natural units).
proper-time-curved-spacetime.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of flat spacetime (where the metric tensor g_{μν} approaches the Minkowski metric 2η_{μν}), the formula simplifies. For a particle moving with constant velocity in one spatial dimension, γ = 1/√{1 - v^2/c^2} is the Lorentz factor, and the proper time is 	au = Δt/γ = Δt √{1 - v^2/c^2}, where Δt is the coordinate time. As the velocity v approaches zero, the proper time approaches the coordinate time Δt, as expected in the non-relativistic limit. As v approaches c, the proper time approaches zero for any finite coordinate time interval, indicating time dilation.

force-field-psi-nabla-phi.title: Force field in terms of a scalar potential and a scalar function
force-field-psi-nabla-phi.conceptual_definition: This formula describes how a force field F can be derived from the product of a scalar quantity ψ and the gradient of another scalar quantity φ. The gradient operator ∇ indicates the direction and magnitude of the steepest ascent of the scalar field φ, effectively turning a scalar potential into a vector field (the force). The scalar multiplier ψ then scales this resultant force field.
force-field-psi-nabla-phi.intuitive_summary: A force field can be generated by scaling the direction and magnitude of steepest ascent of a scalar potential by another scalar quantity.
force-field-psi-nabla-phi.interpretation: The equation F = ψ ∇φ expresses a vector force field F as the product of a scalar field ψ and the gradient of another scalar field φ. The scalar field φ, often referred to as a scalar potential, defines a landscape where its gradient, ∇φ, points in the direction of the greatest increase of φ and its magnitude represents the rate of that increase. This gradient vector field has units of potential per unit length (e.g., V/m for electric potential, J/m for gravitational potential). The scalar field ψ acts as a proportionality constant or a scaling factor at each point in space, modifying the magnitude and potentially the direction (if ψ is negative) of the force. The units of ψ must be such that when multiplied by the units of ∇φ, the result is a force (e.g., Newtons). For example, if φ represents electric potential (Volts, V) and ψ represents electric charge (Coulombs, C), then F would be an electric force (Newtons, N). In this case, ψ∇φ is essentially charge times the electric field E = -∇φ (if we account for the negative sign inherent in the definition of electric field from electric potential), leading to F = qE. In a more general context, ψ might represent a density or a coupling constant.
force-field-psi-nabla-phi.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from the concept of potentials in physics, where conservative force fields can be derived from a scalar potential function. The gradient operation ∇ is fundamentally related to how a scalar quantity changes in space. The inclusion of an additional scalar multiplier ψ generalizes this relationship. For instance, in electromagnetism, the electric field E is the negative gradient of the electric potential φ, i.e., E = -∇φ. Then, the force on a charge q is F = qE = -q∇φ. The given formula F = ψ ∇φ can be seen as a generalization where ψ may not be a simple constant charge, and the sign convention might differ depending on the specific physical context. The formula is coordinate-independent, meaning it holds true regardless of the chosen coordinate system, due to the tensorial nature of the gradient and force vector.
force-field-psi-nabla-phi.limits_and_boundary: As the scalar potential φ approaches a constant value everywhere in space, its gradient ∇φ becomes zero, resulting in a zero force field F = 0. If the scalar multiplier ψ approaches zero, the force field F also approaches zero, indicating no force is exerted. Conversely, if ψ becomes very large, the force field magnitude becomes large, scaled by ψ. If the scalar potential φ varies significantly, its gradient ∇φ will have a large magnitude, leading to a strong force field, assuming ψ is non-zero. At spatial infinity, the behavior depends entirely on the asymptotic behavior of both ψ and φ.

\\mathbf{F}.name: Force Field
\\mathbf{F}.description: A vector field that describes the force experienced by a unit test particle or charge at every point in space. Represented in Newtons (N).

\\psi.name: Scalar Multiplier Field
\\psi.description: A scalar field that scales the gradient of the scalar potential. Its units depend on the specific physical context to yield a force. In the context of electromagnetism where \phi is electric potential (V) and \nabla\phi is related to the electric field (V/m), \psi could represent charge (C) to make \mathbf{F} have units of N, thus \psi would have units of C.

\\nabla.name: Gradient Operator
\\nabla.description: The vector differential operator that describes the rate and direction of greatest increase of a scalar field. In Cartesian coordinates, \nabla = (\partial/\partial x, \partial/\partial y, \partial/\partial z).

\\phi.name: Scalar Potential
\\phi.description: A scalar field that defines a potential energy per unit of some quantity (e.g., per unit charge for electric potential, per unit mass for gravitational potential). Its gradient indicates the direction and magnitude of the force. In SI units, potential energy is measured in Joules (J).

angular-momentum-quantum-number-two.title: Angular momentum quantum number or orbital index is two
angular-momentum-quantum-number-two.conceptual_definition: The formula \(l=2\) specifies that the angular momentum quantum number, denoted by \(l\), has a value of 2. In quantum mechanics, the angular momentum quantum number is a fundamental property of an electron (or other particle) within an atom, describing the shape of its orbital. The integer values of \(l\) correspond to different subshells: \(l=0\) for s subshells (spherical shape), \(l=1\) for p subshells (dumbbell shape), \(l=2\) for d subshells (more complex shapes, often depicted as cloverleafs), and so on.
angular-momentum-quantum-number-two.intuitive_summary: An electron in an orbital with a shape designated by \(l=2\) possesses a specific amount of orbital angular momentum, corresponding to a d-orbital.
angular-momentum-quantum-number-two.interpretation: In this formula, \(l\) is the angular momentum quantum number, a dimensionless integer that quantifies the magnitude of the orbital angular momentum of an electron. The value \(l=2\) indicates that the electron resides in a d subshell. The orbital angular momentum itself is related to \(l\) by the formula \(L = \hbar \sqrt{l(l+1)}\), where \(\hbar\) is the reduced Planck constant. For \(l=2\), this means the magnitude of the orbital angular momentum is \(L = \hbar \sqrt{2(2+1)} = \hbar \sqrt{6}\). This value of \(l\) dictates the spatial distribution of the electron's probability density, leading to the characteristic shapes of d orbitals.
angular-momentum-quantum-number-two.symmetry_origin: The angular momentum quantum number \(l\) arises from the symmetry of the central potential in the Schrödinger equation, specifically from the angular part of the Laplacian operator in spherical coordinates. Its quantization is a consequence of the boundary conditions imposed on the wave function, ensuring that it remains finite and single-valued as the angular coordinates \(\theta\) and \(\phi\) are varied. Conservation of angular momentum in systems with central potentials is a key physical principle that leads to the quantization of this quantity.
angular-momentum-quantum-number-two.limits_and_boundary: The angular momentum quantum number \(l\) must be a non-negative integer (\(l=0, 1, 2, ...\)). There is no theoretical upper limit to \(l\) in general, but in a specific atom, \(l\) is limited by the principal quantum number \(n\) such that \(0 \le l < n\). As \(l\) approaches infinity (a hypothetical scenario not realized in bound atomic states), the orbital angular momentum magnitude \(L\) would also approach infinity, and the electron's wave function would become increasingly delocalized and spread out over space.

l.name: Angular Momentum Quantum Number
l.description: The angular momentum quantum number, often called the orbital index or azimuthal quantum number. It is a non-negative integer that characterizes the magnitude of the orbital angular momentum of an electron in an atom.  The value \(l=2\) corresponds to a d subshell.
